name: Datalizer
tagline: Business intelligence tooling for slicing warehouse and database data into cross-tabs, pivots and dashboards.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The core of any pivot and dashboard tool is a query builder over a columnar engine, and that part is genuinely a weekend project now: DuckDB plus a chart library gets you cross-tabs, drilldowns and exports without much drama. What does not fall out of one session is everything around it: connectors to the ten databases your data actually lives in, row-level permissions, a shared semantic layer so two people agree on what revenue means, and scheduled refresh that does not silently break. If you are one person analysing your own CSVs and one Postgres, the DIY version is often better than the product because you can write raw SQL when the UI fights you. If the tool is holding a team's reporting definitions, the value is the governance and the fact that nobody has to trust your laptop. Treat this as buildable for personal use and not buildable as an internal standard.
coreLoopDIY: A local app that connects to your CSVs, Parquet files or a read-only Postgres, lets you build cross-tabs and charts by picking dimensions and measures, and saves those views so you can reload and export them.
requirements: A local data source: CSV, Parquet, or read-only Postgres credentials
Comfort writing at least a little SQL when the UI runs out of ideas
whatYouLose: Prebuilt connectors to the databases and SaaS apps you did not think about
A shared semantic layer, so metric definitions live in your head instead of in one governed place
Row-level and column-level permissions for anyone but you
Scheduled refresh, alerting and delivery that runs when your machine is asleep
Vendor support and an audit trail when a number in a board deck is questioned
moatNotes: Reporting tools get sticky the moment a metric definition inside them becomes the company's official answer. Migrating that is politics, not engineering.
whyPeopleStillPay: Nobody buys BI for the pivot table, they buy it so that the sales number in the Monday meeting is the same number everyone else sees, sourced from a system that IT signed off on and that keeps working when the person who built it leaves. Paid tools also absorb the boring parts: dozens of maintained connectors, refresh scheduling, access control, and a support contract to point at when the report breaks the morning of a board call. A personal build wins on flexibility and cost and loses badly on being trustworthy to other people.
notes: The query engine is free now, so most of what you are paying for is agreement between colleagues.
prompt:
Build a local, single-user BI and pivot tool. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Python 3.11, DuckDB for all querying, Streamlit for the UI, Plotly for charts.
- Everything runs with `streamlit run app.py` on localhost. No Docker required.

Data sources:
- Point the app at a local folder of CSV and Parquet files; register each file as a DuckDB view named after the file.
- Optional read-only Postgres source using the DuckDB postgres extension, with the connection string read from .env (PG_URL). Never hardcode credentials, ship a .env.example.
- Show a schema browser: tables, columns, inferred types, row counts.

Core analysis loop:
- Pick one table or view. Choose row dimensions (multiple), column dimensions (up to two), and measures with aggregations: sum, avg, min, max, count, count distinct.
- Add filters per column: equality, IN list, numeric ranges, date ranges.
- Render a cross-tab with subtotals and a grand total. Support drilldown: clicking a row expands the next dimension level.
- Toggle between table view and chart view: bar, line, stacked bar, scatter.
- Build the SQL as a readable string, always display it, and let the user edit it and run the edited version.

Saved views and export:
- Save a view definition as YAML in ./views/, load it back from a dropdown, delete it.
- Export the current result as CSV and XLSX.

Explicitly out of scope: user accounts, permissions, sharing links, scheduled refresh, email delivery, a semantic layer, write-back to sources.

Deliverables: app.py plus small modules for source registration, query building and view persistence, a requirements.txt, a .env.example, sample CSVs in ./data/, and a README with a 60 second quickstart. Include pytest tests for the SQL builder covering aggregation, filters and subtotals.
